title: GPU runtime profiling: NVTX traces, prefetch heuristics & hybrid kernel fallback
topics: NVTX tracing and NVTX region annotation
summary: Deep technical session focusing on root-cause analysis for variability in token latency under load. Reviewed NVTX traces and proposed a benchmarking plan: run TRT-LLM and vLLM with identical model quant profiles, NVTX annotated workloads, and KV cache warm/cold scenarios across their on-prem GPU cluster. Identified prefetch tuning, CUDA graph replay timing, and kernel fallback thresholds as primary areas to optimize for predictable tail latency.
next_steps: Redwood to share annotated NVTX + checkpointed traces and a reference benchmark harness (shared: /s/nvtx-bench-deck)
Orchid to run 3 baseline runs (cold KV, warm KV, high-concurrency mixed) and upload logs to shared bucket
Schedule follow-up week-of 2026-11-16 to review results and decide pilot config (Dedicated vs Private)
action_items: Owner: Priya Nair | Item: Export NVTX regions with high-res timestamps + include cuda graph replay markers | Due: 2026-11-09
Owner: Evan Brooks | Item: Run baseline TRT-LLM + vLLM runs with deterministic seeds and attach logs | Due: 2026-11-11
Owner: Kai Matsuda | Item: Provide cluster topology (GPU types, NVLink, PCIe layout) and kernel driver versions | Due: 2026-11-08
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to dig into the variability you saw on the last run. um, real quick intros?
[00:12] Maria Gonzales: Maria here, CTO at Orchid, thanks. Evan's on the call and Kai for infra.
[00:18] Jordan Lee: perfect. Priya from our SE team will lead the profiling part.
[00:22] Priya Nair: hi all, yeah, I pulled the nvtx traces you uploaded — thanks for that — they helped a lot to map kernel transitions. just to set expectations, we'll try to correlate NVTX regions to cuda graph replay behavior and KV cache eviction patterns.
[00:38] Evan Brooks: quick context — our production has 8xA100 per node, nvlink enabled, but we've noticed tail spikes under mixed small/medium requests. sometimes 95th jumps 2x for 1 token.
[00:50] Kai Matsuda: we run TRT-LLM builds for some models and vLLM for others, trying to see which is more stable. also using 4-bit quant on a few of them.
[01:05] Priya Nair: ok, perfect. from the traces what looks interesting is there are repeated kernel fallback events — profiles show a fast path kernel then a larger kernel after eviction. that indicates hybrid kernel selection is flipping at runtime.
[01:20] Jordan Lee: when you say "fallback" can you explain the heuristic? like is it sequence-length based or memory-pressure triggered?
[01:26] Priya Nair: good q. usually the runtime will pick an optimized kernel if predicted sequence and kv cache fit certain thresholds. but when KV prefetch misses or CUDA graph replay occurs late, the runtime often falls back to a generic kernel to be safe. the NVTX markers show a 30-100ms gap before the fallback kernel.
[01:47] Maria Gonzales: that matches our observations — a cold prefix then many parallel short sessions seem to push it over.
[01:53] Evan Brooks: also, sometimes cuda graph replay fails and then we see a full recompile on the fly? transcription: it said "recom- recompile" sometimes.
[02:03] Priya Nair: yes, and compiles / graph replay can add jitter. one point: TRT-LLM's graph capture and TRT kernel selection is more aggressive — it can get better peak throughput, but when a mismatch happens (like unexpected kv shape) it will reinitialize, causing a larger spike. vLLM tends to be a bit more conservative, so smaller spikes but more consistent steady latency.
[02:22] Kai Matsuda: is that a driver version thing, or model artifact? we run driver 525.x.
[02:28] Priya Nair: driver can matter, but we saw similar behavior across 525 and 535 in labs. the main difference is the graph replay timing and how kernels are registered. also cudagraph replay order matters — if capture runs before KV warmup finishes, the captured graph doesn't include prefetch ops and later mismatches happen.
[02:48] Jordan Lee: so sequence: capture occurs, KV cache warms after, later requests hit different path and cause fallback. how to force a consistent capture?
[02:57] Priya Nair: a couple options. pre-warm sequence by issuing synthetic prefix tokens to prime KV before capture; annotate NVTX regions to include prefetch and confirm prefetch completed before capture; or disable graph capture during initial warmup. each has tradeoffs.
[03:13] Maria Gonzales: what's the impact on throughput if we disable capture for warmup?
[03:17] Priya Nair: small steady-state penalty, but you avoid expensive reinitialization. so overall better 95/99th if your workload has high variability.
[03:27] Evan Brooks: can we instrument the scheduler to delay capture until KV cache hit-rate > threshold?
[03:33] Priya Nair: yes. that's basically what we're recommending — add a prefetch completeness check and only capture when hit-rate looks stable. we can add a flag in the runtime to check KV warm ratio.
[03:42] Jordan Lee: ok. let's talk quantization — you mentioned 4-bit. any observable differences between TRT-LLM and vLLM for int4?
[03:49] Priya Nair: int4 quant can change kernel selection. TRT often uses specialized int4 kernels which are very fast but more brittle; if there's any layout mismatch (per-channel scale differences) it falls back to non-optimized fp16 path or a slower int gemm, causing latency spikes. vLLM's int4 support is more conservative and often uses emulation layers that are slower but consistent.
[04:12] Kai Matsuda: our logs show periodic "mixed-precision fallback" messages. are those coming from the runtime or from cuBLAS?
[04:18] Priya Nair: usually runtime. it will try optimized primitives, then call into cuBLAS or Triton if necessary. nvprof / nsight shows the switch. NVTX helps to annotate those transitions.
[04:30] Evan Brooks: you mentioned NVTX markers — what should we add to traces? we added some regions but maybe not enough detail.
[04:36] Priya Nair: good point. include: prefetch start/end, KV lookup start/end, cuda graph capture start/end, kernel selection decision point, and post-kernel commit. also annotate user-level request id to correlate with logs. we find 10-20ms markers help.
[04:52] Maria Gonzales: ok we'll add more detailed NVTX spans. is there a recommended sample rate for logging? we don't want to fill disks.
[04:58] Priya Nair: keep nvtx in-memory and only dump on errors or schedule short runs. for normal profiling, 1:10 sampling is fine. for full runs, use dedicated nodes to avoid noise.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: let's pivot to batching — mixed small/medium requests were causing the headroom issues, right?
[05:16] Priya Nair: yes. batching strategy interacts with kernel selection. smaller batches favor low-latency kernels whereas larger batches shift to high-throughput kernels. the runtime's continuous batching tries to balance, but eviction and KV miss patterns can force it to re-evaluate. we saw a pattern where concurrent small sessions created micro-batches that triggered a path mismatch.
[05:37] Evan Brooks: are there heuristics to prioritize latency SLOs over throughput?
[05:41] Priya Nair: yes — configure target latency thresholds per model route; runtime will prefer smaller batch windows and lower batching depth to favor latency. you trade tokens/sec. Redwood Optimize can suggest those values based on your traffic mix.
[05:54] Maria Gonzales: we want both low cost and strict 200ms SLO for 95th. is that realistic?
[05:59] Priya Nair: possible with tuning: prefetching KV aggressively, pinned kernels for common paths, and conservative capture windows. sometimes Dedicated capacity helps because you don't share noisy neighbors and can tune kernel placement.
[06:13] Jordan Lee: customers sometimes ask about on-prem VPC differences — how much do these behaviors change between hosted and private?
[06:20] Priya Nair: on-prem differences come down to network/NVLink topology, driver versions, and kernel scheduling. in our hosted fleet we can control firmware and drivers; on-prem you'll likely see more variability unless you standardize stack. also KMS/HSM operations for keys can add latency if called synchronously.
[06:35] Kai Matsuda: we do KMS calls for tokenization metadata — are those synchronous in Redwood private?
[06:40] Jordan Lee: we can configure async KMS or local cache. we'll share recommended patterns.
[06:44] Evan Brooks: back to CUDA graphs: you mentioned replay timing — are there best practices to annotate replay boundaries so we know when a graph was used vs fallback?
[06:53] Priya Nair: annotate capture_start, capture_end, replay_start, replay_end, and a unique graph id. also emit a "graph_mismatch" NVTX when fallback happens. then correlate with kernel selection markers.
[07:07] Maria Gonzales: can Redwood provide a small harness that does these annotations out of the box?
[07:11] Priya Nair: yes, we'll share a lightweight harness that includes NVTX wrappers and simple synthetic prefetch patterns. shared: /s/nvtx-harness.
[07:19] Jordan Lee: perfect. want to walk through a trace now? Evan uploaded one earlier — "run-20261029-3".
[07:26] Evan Brooks: yeah, should be attached in the deck.
[07:29] Priya Nair: looking at the trace: at [NVTX:prefetch_end] there's a gap of ~42ms until the capture. during that gap another parallel request arrived and allocation pressure caused an eviction of older KV entries. subsequent replay then captured state without those entries. that's the mismatch.
[07:51] Kai Matsuda: so pipeline timing — our prefetch isn't synchronized across worker threads. is there a cheap lockless way to coordinate?
[07:58] Priya Nair: you can use a simple epoch counter per request and a prefetch token. only the capture thread needs to check the epoch, not block all workers. cheap, and avoids full mutexes.
[08:08] Jordan Lee: from a runtime change perspective — would Redwood add an integration hook or is this something Orchid should implement in their layer?
[08:15] Priya Nair: we can add an optional runtime hook to enforce capture gating by epoch. it's not invasive and can be gated behind a config flag for Private/Dedicated deployments.
[08:25] Evan Brooks: sounds good. timeline?
[08:27] Priya Nair: we can prototype in 2 weeks, then test on your baseline.
[08:31] Maria Gonzales: excellent. can we talk briefly about kernel-level metrics to watch?
[08:35] Priya Nair: yes: per-kernel latency, launch overhead, memory copy times, and occupancy. CPU-side metrics: time-to-dispatch and thread-loop latencies. also watch for temps and power capping events which can throttle.
[08:49] Kai Matsuda: we saw PCIe throttle warnings once when multi-jobing. could that explain spikes?
[08:54] Priya Nair: absolutely. if your GPU is throttled due to thermal/power or PCIe stalls, kernel durations blow out. NVTX won't show thermal, but system telemetry will. correlate with dmesg and nvidia-smi logs.
[09:08] Jordan Lee: any surprises on kernel selection differences between TRT-LLM and vLLM?
[09:12] Priya Nair: TRT-LLM often wins for large batch throughput and fp16/int8 specialized kernels. vLLM is better at variable sequence workloads because it manages KV layout more conservatively and avoids some graph-capture shortcuts. For Orchid's mixed short sessions, vLLM may hit fewer catastrophic fallbacks but slightly lower peak throughput.
[09:33] Evan Brooks: interesting — so maybe route chat-like flows to vLLM and bulk generation to TRT-LLM?
[09:38] Priya Nair: exactly — smart routing by request type reduces tail risk. Redwood routing policies can do that based on headers or prompt metadata.
[09:47] Maria Gonzales: can routing be per-tenant or per-route? we have multi-tenant clusters.
[09:51] Jordan Lee: per-route and per-customer routing is supported; you can pin model variants by route.
[09:56] Evan Brooks: what about quantization switching at runtime? switching quant profiles mid-run seems risky.
[10:01] Priya Nair: runtime switching should be avoided; deploy a variant per quant profile and route accordingly. that avoids in-flight kernel mismatches.
[10:10] Kai Matsuda: ok. practical question: when we run the recommended baseline (cold KV, warm KV, high-concurrency mixed), what exact commands/logging should we use?
[10:19] Priya Nair: we'll give a script. key bits: enable NVTX regions listed earlier, set deterministic seeds, flush caches between runs, record nsight/nvprof output on a dedicated node, and capture runtime metrics (token/sec, enqueue latency, kernel counts). we'll include a metrics exporter to push to your prometheus.
[10:36] Jordan Lee: good. any thoughts on throughput headroom math? we want to size Dedicated pools.
[10:41] Priya Nair: use the 95th latency under mixed load as sizing baseline, then add safety headroom (recommended 1.3x for variable workloads). if TRT-LLM is used for bulk inference, size for peak tokens/sec then route small sessions elsewhere.
[10:55] Evan Brooks: can you quantify KV prefetch traffic — is it a lot of PCIe bandwidth?
[10:59] Priya Nair: depends on kv size and prefetch granularity. small keys are cheap, but large context windows push memory traffic. measure with nvlink counters. sometimes prefetching entire segments is overkill — selective prefetch by token locality helps.
[11:15] Maria Gonzales: selective prefetch sounds good — we can add heuristics in our tokenization layer.
[11:19] Priya Nair: yes, and annotate what you prefetch in NVTX for trace correlation.
[11:24] Jordan Lee: let's go through the uploaded trace annotations again — Priya, call out the exact time ranges that show the mismatch.
[11:30] Priya Nair: Sure. in run-20261029-3 at NVTX timestamp 00:12:34.210 we see prefetch_end, then at 00:12:34.252 capture_start, capture_end at 00:12:34.270, then at 00:12:34.315 a new request arrives triggering eviction, then at 00:12:34.360 replay_start which lacks the prefetched kv page. the fallback kernel executes at 00:12:34.414 and lasts 64ms instead of expected 12ms. so it's a 52ms penalty.
[12:03] Evan Brooks: wow ok. we'll correlate those timestamps with our logs.
[12:07] Kai Matsuda: are there flags to make capture atomic? like freeze scheduling briefly?
[12:12] Priya Nair: avoid freezing whole node — we recommend capture gating (epoch token) not a global freeze. freezing introduces latency for other requests.
[12:21] Jordan Lee: quick check — any security/compliance flags with NVTX or traces in Private deployments?
[12:26] Priya Nair: only if you ship traces off-box. keep traces within your VPC and scrub PII. Redwood can accept sanitized traces over a secure bucket, or you can host the harness locally.
[12:38] Maria Gonzales: we'll scrub customer IDs.
[12:41] Jordan Lee: good. switching gears: you mentioned power capping earlier. do cloud providers do that often?
[12:47] Priya Nair: sometimes, especially on shared instances; Dedicated avoids noisy neighbor power caps. On-prem can also have aggressive power policies. monitor and set constraints in your scheduler.
[12:58] Evan Brooks: ok. any guidance about kernel launch overheads we should measure? the trace shows frequent small kernels.
[13:05] Priya Nair: small kernels cause high launch overhead relative to compute. group ops where possible or use fused kernels. TRT-LLM does more fusion but is brittle; vLLM is more modular.
[13:18] Maria Gonzales: is fusion safe with int4?
[13:21] Priya Nair: usually yes but verify scales; fusion assumes identical quant params. if you have mixed scale factors per layer, fusion can be wrong and cause fallbacks.
[13:33] Jordan Lee: we need to get you the cluster topology and some sample logs. Kai, can you share the driver/kernel info now?
[13:39] Kai Matsuda: yes, we run CUDA 12.1, driver 535.86, Linux 5.15, A100S. I'll upload the nvlink topology output.
[13:47] Evan Brooks: and I'll run the baseline scripts once we get Priya's harness.
[13:51] Priya Nair: great. one more note: watch for memory fragmentation. repeated allocations across captures can fragment device memory and later force full memcpy paths. periodic defrag or long-lived memory pools helps.
[14:06] Jordan Lee: interesting. do you have a small test that simulates fragmentation?
[14:10] Priya Nair: yes, the harness includes an allocate/free pattern to stress fragmentation. we'll provide that too.
[14:18] Maria Gonzales: ok, practical next steps recap?
[14:21] Jordan Lee: Priya will share harness + deck, Orchid will run baseline, Kai will share topology/versions, then follow-up meeting week-of Nov 16.
[14:29] Evan Brooks: sounds good.
[14:31] Maria Gonzales: quick Q — around A/B routing: can we do canary on small percent to vet TRT-LLM for certain customers?
[14:37] Jordan Lee: yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts by route/model. you can set percent and fallback policies.
[14:43] Priya Nair: and set auto-fallback to vLLM if token latency exceeds threshold.
[14:48] Evan Brooks: perfect. one more question — how do we capture kernel-level perf counters? nsight?
[14:53] Priya Nair: nsight or nvprof (legacy) and CUPTI counters. nsight systems for timeline + CUPTI for counters. we can share recommended counter set.
[15:03] Jordan Lee: ok let's switch to the point about quant regression monitoring — is there an eval hook Redwood suggests?
[15:08] Priya Nair: yes, Redwood Optimize can run evals on a holdout set comparing outputs (perplexity, exact-match, and a small set of human-checked prompts). we recommend automated regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[15:24] Maria Gonzales: we'll want that. compliance needs reproducible evals.
[15:29] Jordan Lee: noted. any outstanding blockers from Orchid?
[15:33] Evan Brooks: only time — we'll need a week to run baselines.
[15:36] Kai Matsuda: I'll share the topology and driver info by Monday.
[15:40] Priya Nair: I'll push the harness and annotated NVTX template today.
[15:44] Jordan Lee: great. final quick note: when you run traces, please attach both NVTX dumps and runtime logs; the id mapping really helps.
[15:52] Maria Gonzales: will do. thanks everyone.
[15:55] Jordan Lee: thanks — we'll follow up with the shared links and schedule.
[16:00] Speaker 6: (auto-transcript) overlapping chatter — end.
[16:05] -- End of transcript (approx)

Notes on transcript: transcription contains some imperfections: product names intermittently mis-transcribed ("TRT-LLM" as "Tensor-R-T LLM"), and some timestamps derived from NVTX markers. References to shared artifacts: shared: /s/nvtx-bench-deck, /s/nvtx-harness (these are placeholders).
